title: Query Builder to Parameterized SQL
prompt: Turn a query spec into a parameterized PostgreSQL-style statement. The spec is `{ table, columns?, where?, orderBy?, limit?, offset? }`. Output `{ ok: true, sql, params }` shaped as `SELECT <cols> FROM "<table>"` followed, when present and non-empty, by ` WHERE <conditions joined by " AND ">`, ` ORDER BY "<col>" ASC|DESC, ...` (direction defaults to asc), ` LIMIT $n`, ` OFFSET $n`. Missing or empty `columns` means `*`. Identifiers (table and every column name) must match `/^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/` and are wrapped in double quotes; otherwise return `{ ok: false, error: "Invalid identifier: <name>" }`. Values are never written into the SQL: each one is pushed to `params` and referenced as `$1`, `$2`, ... in order of appearance. Conditions `{ column, op, value }`: comparison ops `= != < <= > >=` render as `"col" <op> $n`; `like` renders `"col" LIKE $n`; `in` expands to `"col" IN ($1, $2)`, an empty array becomes `1 = 0`, and a non-array is the error `"IN requires an array: <col>"`. A `null` value with `=` is `"col" IS NULL`, with `!=` is `"col" IS NOT NULL`, and with any other op is the error `"Cannot compare <col> with null using <op>"`. `limit` and `offset` must be non-negative integers, else `"Invalid limit"` / `"Invalid offset"`. Build clauses in the order above and report the first error you meet.

explanation.beginner: Build the statement piece by piece. Keep a `params` array and a small `bind(value)` helper that pushes the value and returns its placeholder, `$` plus the new length. Every value goes through bind, so the user's text never becomes part of the SQL itself; that is the whole defence against SQL injection. Column and table names cannot be placeholders in SQL, so they get a different defence: allow only letters, digits, and underscores, and wrap them in double quotes. Then handle the special cases one at a time: `null` needs `IS NULL` because `= NULL` is never true in SQL, an `IN` list gets one placeholder per item, and an empty `IN` list becomes `1 = 0` because `IN ()` is a syntax error. Stop at the first problem by throwing a small error and catching it once at the end.
explanation.junior: The design point is the split between values (bound parameters) and identifiers (allow-listed and quoted). Parameter numbering must follow textual order across all clauses, including LIMIT and OFFSET, which is why a single shared `bind` closure beats computing indexes per clause. SQL's three-valued logic is why `col = NULL` silently matches nothing, and why `<` with null is rejected rather than guessed. `1 = 0` for an empty IN keeps the statement valid and returns no rows, matching what Knex and Prisma do. Throwing a private `QueryError` subclass and catching only it keeps genuine bugs visible. Complexity is linear in the spec size. In production you would also cap `limit`, map allowed sort columns explicitly (users choosing arbitrary sort columns can defeat indexes), and use the driver's own parameter style (`?` for MySQL/SQLite).
